title: Rationing
story:
Sticky note on monitor 3, Amara's handwriting:

"cruncher went into a loop at 3am, spawned a few hundred processes and took the whole box with it. sorry!!

can you box it in? 256 MB of RAM, half a CPU, 64 processes max.
DO NOT restart it -- the glacier job is 80% done and I wrote the checkpoint file by hand. -- A."

Beneath it, in red pen, Wren has underlined "whole box" twice.
objectives: Limit the running container `cruncher` to 256 MB of memory
Limit it to at most 64 processes
Do not recreate it: `/tmp/checkpoint` inside the container must survive
startingState: Container `cruncher` (alpine:3.20) runs with no limits at all, and holds a checkpoint in `/tmp/checkpoint`.
hints: Resource limits are not only for new containers; Docker can change them on a running one. Restarting or recreating `cruncher` would lose the checkpoint that only exists inside it, so look for a command that edits a live container.
`docker update` accepts `--memory`, `--cpus` and `--pids-limit`. When you set a memory limit on a container that had none, set `--memory-swap` to the same value so swap does not exceed it.

```bash
docker update --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 64 cruncher
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}' cruncher
```

commands: docker run -d --name cruncher alpine:3.20 sleep infinity

validation.description: The original container (with its checkpoint) was not recreated

debrief: Memory, CPU and process limits keep one runaway container from starving everything else on the host, and `docker update` applies them live without touching the container's state. Pro tip: `--pids-limit` is the cheap defence against fork bombs, and `docker stats` shows whether a limit is actually being hit.
